title: Bites
path: First Aid Management of Patients with Medical and Surgical Emergencies

headings.title: Introduction and Classification of Bites
headings.content:
Bite injuries represent a common yet complex presentation in Nigerian emergency departments and primary healthcare centres. They span a wide spectrum of severity, ranging from superficial abrasions caused by domestic pets to life-threatening trauma from venomous snakes or wild animals. Healthcare providers must recognize that human bites carry a uniquely high risk of severe infection due to the dense and diverse microbial flora residing in the human oral cavity. 

- **Animal bites**: Usually inflicted by dogs, cats, or wild fauna, often resulting in crush injuries, punctures, or tearing of skin and underlying tissues.
- **Human bites**: Frequently occur during altercations or accidental contact, characterized by high bacterial loads including *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Eikenella corrodens*.
- **Venomous snake bites**: Prevalent in rural agricultural communities across Nigeria, injecting toxic enzymes that cause local tissue destruction and systemic coagulopathy.

headings.title: Pathophysiology of Local and Systemic Damage
headings.content:
When teeth penetrate the skin barrier, mechanical trauma occurs alongside microbial inoculation. Puncture wounds seal over quickly, trapping bacteria in a low-oxygen environment ideal for anaerobic growth. In the case of venomous snakes, hemotoxins or neurotoxins disrupt normal physiological processes, leading to local necrosis, hemolysis, or paralysis. 

Inflammation develops rapidly around the bite site. Edema compromises local microcirculation, worsening tissue ischemia and increasing susceptibility to secondary bacterial colonization. Systemic absorption of toxins or bacterial endotoxins can precipitate systemic inflammatory response syndrome, acute kidney injury, or disseminated intravascular coagulation if intervention is delayed.

headings.title: Assessment, Triage, and History Taking
headings.content:
Immediate triage determines the urgency of care based on airway stability, hemodynamic status, and anatomical location of the bite. A comprehensive history establishes the time of the incident, the species of the animal, vaccination status (especially tetanus and rabies), and the patient's underlying health conditions such as diabetes or immunosuppression.

Physical examination evaluates neurovascular status distal to the wound. Sensation, pulses, capillary refill, and active movement must be documented before administering local anesthesia or performing wound exploration. Neglecting this baseline assessment can obscure subsequent nerve or tendon damage.

headings.title: First Aid and Pre-Hospital Management
headings.content:
Effective first aid reduces microbial load and slows toxin absorption. Immediate and thorough irrigation of the wound with copious amounts of clean water or normal saline is the single most effective step in preventing infection.

- **Wound irrigation**: Use high-pressure flushing where possible to dislodge debris and bacteria.
- **Tourniquets**: Generally discouraged for snakebites as they cause severe localized ischemia and gangrene; pressure immobilization is preferred for elapid bites.
- **Traditional remedies**: Avoid applying native herbs, black stone, or saliva to the wound, as these introduce harmful contaminants and delay professional care.

headings.title: Hospital Medical and Surgical Interventions
headings.content:
Hospital management combines pharmacotherapy with surgical consultation depending on tissue involvement. Prophylactic antibiotics are frequently prescribed for high-risk wounds, such as cat bites, human bites, and deep punctures, even before clinical signs of infection appear.

Tetanus toxoid and, when indicated, human tetanus immunoglobulin are administered based on immunization history. Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis is initiated immediately if the biting animal is suspected of carrying the virus. Surgical debridement is performed under aseptic conditions to excise necrotic tissue, irrigate deep compartments, and repair damaged tendons or nerves.

headings.title: Infection Control and Prevention of Complications
headings.content:
Monitoring for secondary complications is a core nursing responsibility. Signs of developing cellulitis, lymphangitis, or abscess formation include increasing erythema, localized warmth, purulent discharge, and systemic fever. 

Wounds left open to heal by secondary intention require careful aseptic dressing changes to promote granulation tissue formation while preventing hospital-acquired superinfections. Nurses must educate patients on completing their full course of prescribed antibiotics rather than stopping when surface symptoms subside.

headings.title: Patient Education and Discharge Planning
headings.content:
Comprehensive discharge planning ensures continuity of care once the patient leaves the healthcare facility. Nurses instruct patients on proper wound care techniques, hand hygiene, and signs of complications that require immediate return to the clinic.

Education must also address animal safety and prevention strategies, particularly for children who are most vulnerable to animal bites. For snakebite survivors, guidance includes environmental modifications around the home to reduce rodent attraction and snake habitats.
